source.title_on_document: Effects of AI-generated images in visual art education on students' classroom engagement, self-efficacy and cognitive load

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Data availability statement: "No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study." (p. 12).

paper_design_summary: 78 fifth-grade students from two classes (39 and 39) at one primary school in Shandong Province, China, were split into a treatment and a control group (the abstract says randomly assigned; the introduction calls the study quasi-experimental). In a cartoon-painting lesson, the teacher's PowerPoint examples were Stable Diffusion images made by a research assistant for the treatment group and classical cartoon artworks for the control group; students did not use AI themselves and painted with pencils and watercolors. Three teachers rated each Task 2 painting on a 1-5 rubric (technical skill, adherence to theme, composition and design, creativity and originality, effort and improvement); questionnaires measured engagement, self-efficacy, and cognitive load.

studies.label: Classroom experiment: AI-generated vs classical example images in a fifth-grade cartoon-painting lesson

assignment.what_was_assigned: Source of the example images in the teacher's instructional slides for Task 2: AI-generated (Stable Diffusion) images vs classical artworks of iconic cartoon characters.
assignment.quote: Seventy-eight fifth-grade students were randomly assigned to a treatment group (n = 39) and a control group (n = 39).
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract. Contrast: p. 2, Introduction ("we conducted a quasi-experimental study involving 78 fifth-grade students, divided into control and treatment groups"); p. 4, Methods, Participants ("drawn from two classes: Class A (39 students) and Class B (39 students)"; "Participants were assigned to either the treatment or control group"). The unit of assignment (student or intact class) is not stated.

arms.name: Treatment (GAI-assisted teaching)
arms.description: Task 2 instruction with PowerPoint slides built from AI-generated images (Stable Diffusion; Fig. 3), produced by a research assistant; students painted by hand with traditional tools.

arms.name: Control (conventional teaching)
arms.description: Same Task 2 instruction by the same teacher with slides built from classical artworks of iconic cartoon characters (Fig. 4); students painted by hand with traditional tools.

participants.exclusions: None reported; every results table shows n = 39 per group.
participants.who: Fifth-grade primary school students, ages 10 to 12 (mean 11.13, SD 0.437), 41 male and 37 female, from two classes (Class A and Class B, 39 each).
participants.country: China (Shandong Province; school is Qingdao Ningxia Road Primary School per affiliations)
participants.quote: This study involved 78 fifth-grade students from a primary school in Shandong Province, China. The participants were drawn from two classes: Class A (39 students) and Class B (39 students), comprising 41 males and 37 females.
participants.locator: p. 4, Methods, Participants; p. 4, Table 1; p. 1, Abstract

ai_tool.name_model: Stable Diffusion (checkpoints shown in Fig. 3: realvisxlV40_v40LightningBakedvae, AnythingXL_xl, cartoonArcadiaSDXLSD1_xenoArcadiaCX)
ai_tool.how_used: AI-generated example images were shown to the treatment group in the teacher's PowerPoint slides during Task 2 instruction. Students did not operate the AI: "a research assistant obtained the AI-generated images for them" (p. 12). Whether the images stayed visible during painting practice is not stated.

task.description: Task 2, "Anthropomorphic Cartoon Character": "Using the anthropomorphism techniques you have learned, create and design a distinct and characteristic anthropomorphic cartoon character", painted with sketching pencils, watercolor paints, and art paper (p. 6).
task.duration: Stage 3 (teacher instruction plus painting practice) lasted about 40 minutes (p. 6); the Participants section describes the module as two 20-minute sessions (p. 4).

outcomes.name: Creativity and Originality (rubric score of Task 2 painting)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric item "Creativity and Originality: How unique and imaginative is the artwork?" scored 1 to 5 by three teachers (two art teachers, one math teacher; Table 8). Rater Z is also the instructor of the experiment (p. 8), although p. 6 states raters were blinded to group. ICC for the composite score averaged across all criteria = 0.847 (p. 11). How rater scores are combined per painting is not stated. The item could also be read as novelty ("unique and imaginative").

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear on two counts. First, the abstract says 78 students were randomly assigned (39/39), but the introduction calls the study quasi-experimental and the Methods say participants came from two classes of 39 each and "were assigned" with no mention of randomization; the groups may be the two intact classes, which would make it either non-random or cluster-randomized with two clusters. Second, students never used AI: the teacher's example images were AI-generated (made by a research assistant) versus classical artworks, so the AI exposure is AI-generated examples supplied in instruction (ideas_supplied) against human-made examples. Criterion 2: 78 students analyzed (39 + 39). Criterion 3: Task 2 paintings rated by three teachers on a rubric item "Creativity and Originality" (Table 9). If the design is judged non-random (intact classes), the study would be quasi_people (observational context).

one_line_finding: Fifth graders taught with AI-generated example images received higher teacher-rated Creativity and Originality scores for their hand-painted cartoon characters than classmates taught with classical examples (4.581, SD 0.444 vs 4.205, SD 0.499, n = 39 each; t = 3.515, p < 0.001; p. 11, Table 9).
open_questions: Was assignment at the student level or by intact class (Class A vs Class B, 39 each)? The abstract says randomly assigned; the introduction says quasi-experimental.
Does showing AI-generated example images in teacher instruction, with no student use of AI, count as AI assistance for criterion 1 (role ideas_supplied, comparison ai_vs_active)?

Were the AI-generated images visible while students painted? Coded ai_available_when_produced = yes because the painting was done in the same 40-minute stage that used the AI examples, but the paper does not say.
Rater Z is the instructor of the experiment (p. 8), which conflicts with the statement that raters were blinded to group assignment (p. 6).
Are the Table 9 p-values one-tailed? For example t = 2.554 with p = 0.006 and n = 78; the paper does not say.
notes: Only outcomes scored on the paintings are listed. The paper also reports questionnaire outcomes that are self-reports and do not qualify: classroom engagement (Tables 3-4), self-efficacy (Tables 5-6), and cognitive load (Table 7). Fig. 2 (p. 5) shows that Task 1 paintings were rated at pretest and that the treatment group had interviews at Stage 4; neither result is reported. The Data analysis section says t-tests and ANCOVA were run on painting scores, but only t-tests appear (Table 9). Text says affective-engagement F = 17.279 (p. 8) while Table 4 prints 17.379. The Discussion (p. 11) describes the rubric results as students' satisfaction with their artworks, although the scores came from teacher raters. One painting per student; the unit is coded participant because Table 9 has n = 39 per group. Table 9 row label is printed as "Creativity and Originalit".
